lessons.title: Innate Versus Adaptive Immunity
body: The immune system has two cooperating arms. Innate immunity is present from birth, responds within minutes to hours, and recognizes broad molecular patterns shared by many microbes. Adaptive immunity depends on lymphocytes whose antigen receptors are assembled by somatic gene rearrangement, so each clone recognizes one specific epitope. It takes days to mount a first response, but it creates memory, so a second encounter is faster, larger and better targeted.

The innate arm begins with barriers: intact skin, mucus and cilia, low gastric pH, lysozyme in tears and saliva, defensins, and the competing normal flora. When barriers are breached, innate cells take over. Neutrophils are the most numerous circulating leukocytes and are short-lived professional phagocytes. Monocytes leave the blood and become tissue macrophages, which clear debris, kill microbes and secrete cytokines. Dendritic cells are the bridge to adaptive immunity because they carry antigen to lymph nodes. Natural killer cells, mast cells, eosinophils and basophils round out the group. Innate lymphoid cells mirror T helper subsets but lack antigen-specific receptors.

Innate cells recognize pathogen-associated molecular patterns, such as lipopolysaccharide, peptidoglycan, flagellin, unmethylated CpG DNA and double-stranded RNA, through germline-encoded pattern recognition receptors. They also sense damage-associated molecular patterns released by injured host cells. Because these receptors are not rearranged, the innate response is fast but has no classical clonal memory, although the idea of trained innate immunity, in which epigenetic changes in monocytes and NK cells alter later responses, is an active research area.

The arms are not independent. Dendritic cells that sense a pathogen upregulate costimulatory molecules and migrate to lymph nodes, which determines whether and how T cells are activated. Antibodies, in turn, recruit complement and phagocytes, directing innate effectors at targets they would otherwise miss. A common exam distinction: the innate response determines the quality of the adaptive response, and the adaptive response amplifies innate killing.

Worked example. A patient steps on a rusty nail. Within minutes, tissue macrophages and mast cells release cytokines, local vessels dilate, and neutrophils arrive within hours. Dendritic cells carry bacterial peptides to a draining lymph node, and by about one week specific T cells and antibody are present. If the patient is exposed again years later, memory B and T cells respond much faster, which is the practical benefit of the adaptive arm and the reason booster vaccination works.

lessons.title: The Complement System
body: Complement is a cascade of plasma and cell-surface proteins, mostly made in the liver, that tags microbes for destruction, recruits phagocytes and can punch holes in membranes. Most components circulate as inactive zymogens and are activated by sequential proteolytic cleavage.

Three pathways converge on cleavage of C3. The classical pathway is started when C1q binds the Fc portions of IgM or clustered IgG that is bound to antigen, so it links adaptive immunity to complement. C1r and C1s then cleave C4 and C2 to form the classical C3 convertase, C4b2a. The lectin pathway is triggered when mannose-binding lectin binds mannose residues on microbes and uses the same C4b2a convertase. The alternative pathway runs continuously at a low level through spontaneous hydrolysis of C3. Factor B and factor D build the convertase C3bBb on microbial surfaces, and properdin stabilizes it. Host cells are protected by regulators such as factor H, decay-accelerating factor (DAF, CD55) and CD59.

C3 convertases cleave C3 into C3a and C3b. C3b is the major opsonin, because phagocytes carry receptors for it, and it also joins the convertase to form C5 convertase. C5 is cleaved into C5a and C5b. C3a and C5a are anaphylatoxins that degranulate mast cells and increase vascular permeability, and C5a is also a strong neutrophil chemoattractant. C5b nucleates assembly of C6, C7, C8 and multiple C9 molecules into the membrane attack complex, which lyses cells. The MAC is particularly important for killing Neisseria species.

The deficiency pattern is a favorite exam topic. C3 deficiency causes severe recurrent pyogenic infections. Deficiency of early classical components (C1, C2, C4) predisposes to immune-complex disease such as lupus, because complement normally helps clear complexes. Deficiency of terminal components C5 through C9 causes recurrent Neisseria infections. C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema, with episodes of swelling without urticaria, low C4, and bradykinin as the mediator, so it does not respond to antihistamines or steroids. Loss of DAF and CD59 on red cells in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), due to an acquired PIGA mutation, allows complement lysis. The C5 inhibitor eculizumab treats PNH but raises the risk of meningococcal disease, so patients need vaccination.

Worked example. A young adult has a second episode of meningococcal meningitis. A total hemolytic complement (CH50) assay is near zero, and C3 and C4 are normal. This pattern points to a terminal component deficiency, because the MAC cannot form even though opsonization works.

lessons.title: Phagocytes and the Inflammatory Response
body: Acute inflammation is the coordinated delivery of plasma proteins and leukocytes to a site of injury or infection. Resident macrophages and mast cells sense the insult and release TNF-alpha, IL-1 and IL-6, plus histamine and prostaglandins. These cause vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, and expression of adhesion molecules on endothelium. The classic signs are rubor, calor, tumor, dolor and loss of function.

Neutrophil extravasation follows a sequence. First, selectins (E-selectin and P-selectin on activated endothelium) bind sialyl Lewis X on neutrophils and cause rolling. Chemokines such as IL-8 (CXCL8) then activate the neutrophil, and integrins (LFA-1 and Mac-1) bind ICAM-1 for firm adhesion. Finally the cell squeezes through the endothelium by diapedesis, called transmigration, and follows chemotactic gradients (C5a, IL-8, bacterial formylated peptides). Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 results from absent CD18, the common integrin beta-2 chain. It causes delayed umbilical cord separation, recurrent infections without pus, and marked neutrophilia, because cells cannot leave the vessel.

Phagocytosis is enhanced by opsonins, mainly IgG and C3b, which bind Fc receptors and complement receptors. The phagosome fuses with lysosomes. The oxidative burst depends on NADPH oxidase, which converts oxygen to superoxide. Superoxide dismutase converts it to hydrogen peroxide, and myeloperoxidase uses hydrogen peroxide and chloride to make hypochlorous acid. Chronic granulomatous disease is caused by defects in NADPH oxidase, most often X-linked CYBB. Patients suffer catalase-positive infections (Staphylococcus aureus, Aspergillus, Burkholderia cepacia, Serratia, Nocardia) and granulomas. The nitroblue tetrazolium test or the dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry assay shows failure of the burst. Catalase-negative organisms are usually handled because they supply their own hydrogen peroxide.

Neutrophils can also extrude chromatin as neutrophil extracellular traps that trap microbes. Systemically, IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-alpha act on the hypothalamus to cause fever through prostaglandin E2, and IL-6 drives hepatic synthesis of acute-phase proteins such as C-reactive protein, fibrinogen, serum amyloid A and hepcidin. The ESR rises mainly because fibrinogen promotes red cell stacking (rouleaux formation), so a high ESR is a nonspecific marker of inflammation rather than a diagnosis. Persistent elevation of serum amyloid A can cause AA amyloidosis.

Worked example. A 6-year-old has recurrent abscesses from Staphylococcus aureus and a liver abscess. Neutrophil counts are normal, and the dihydrorhodamine assay shows no oxidation after stimulation. This is chronic granulomatous disease, and the neutrophils cannot produce superoxide, so intracellular killing of catalase-positive organisms fails even though chemotaxis and phagocytosis are normal.

lessons.title: Pattern Recognition, Interferons and NK Cells
body: Pattern recognition receptors let innate cells detect conserved microbial structures. Toll-like receptors (TLRs) are transmembrane proteins. TLR4, with MD-2 and CD14, senses lipopolysaccharide from Gram-negative bacteria. TLR2 pairs with TLR1 or TLR6 to detect lipoproteins and peptidoglycan, and TLR5 senses flagellin. Endosomal TLRs detect nucleic acids: TLR3 double-stranded RNA, TLR7 and TLR8 single-stranded RNA, and TLR9 unmethylated CpG DNA. Most TLRs signal through MyD88 to activate NF-kappa B and drive transcription of inflammatory cytokines. TLR3 signals through TRIF, and TLR4 can use both adaptors.

Cytosolic sensors extend this surveillance. NOD1 and NOD2 recognize bacterial peptidoglycan fragments, and NOD2 variants are associated with Crohn disease. RIG-I and MDA5 detect viral RNA and signal through MAVS to induce type I interferons. The cGAS-STING pathway senses cytosolic DNA. Inflammasomes, such as NLRP3, assemble in response to danger signals, activate caspase-1, and cleave pro-IL-1 beta and pro-IL-18 into active forms, and can trigger pyroptosis. Gain-of-function mutations in inflammasome components cause autoinflammatory diseases, and colchicine or IL-1 blockade (anakinra, canakinumab) may be used. Gout is an NLRP3-related example because urate crystals activate the inflammasome.

Type I interferons (IFN-alpha and IFN-beta) are made by infected cells and plasmacytoid dendritic cells. They bind the IFNAR receptor, signal through JAK1 and TYK2 with STAT1 and STAT2, and induce an antiviral state: shutdown of protein synthesis, degradation of viral RNA, and upregulation of MHC class I. IFN-gamma, a type II interferon, is made by NK cells and Th1 cells and activates macrophages.

Natural killer cells are large granular lymphocytes that kill virus-infected and tumor cells without prior sensitization. Their activity is balanced between activating receptors and inhibitory receptors, such as KIRs and NKG2A, that recognize self MHC class I. Cells that lose MHC class I, as many viruses and tumors do to escape CD8 T cells, therefore lose the inhibitory signal and become targets. This is the missing self hypothesis. NK cells kill by releasing perforin and granzymes, and they perform antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity through CD16, the Fc gamma receptor III. IL-2, IL-12 and IL-15 activate them, and they are identified by CD56 and CD16 without CD3.

Worked example. A virus downregulates MHC class I to avoid CD8 T cells. CD8 killing falls, but NK cells sense the absent self signal and kill the infected cell, which shows why the two systems complement each other and why viral evasion of one arm often exposes the virus to the other.

lessons.title: MHC and Antigen Presentation
body: T cells cannot see free antigen. Their receptors recognize short peptides displayed on major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules, a property called MHC restriction. In humans the MHC is the HLA region on chromosome 6, and its genes are highly polymorphic, codominantly expressed and inherited together as a haplotype. Siblings have a one in four chance of being HLA identical.

MHC class I (HLA-A, B and C) is expressed on all nucleated cells and on platelets, but not on mature red cells. It presents peptides from proteins made inside the cell, of about 8 to 10 amino acids, to CD8 T cells. The class I heavy chain pairs with beta-2 microglobulin, which is encoded outside the MHC on chromosome 15. Cytosolic proteins are cut by the proteasome, and the peptides are carried into the endoplasmic reticulum by TAP, the transporter associated with antigen processing. Chaperones such as calnexin and tapasin assist loading, and the complex travels to the surface. Interferon gamma enhances this pathway. CD8 binds the alpha-3 domain of class I.

MHC class II (HLA-DP, DQ and DR) is normally expressed only on professional antigen-presenting cells: dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells, plus thymic epithelium. It presents peptides of about 13 to 25 amino acids, derived from extracellular proteins taken up by endocytosis, to CD4 T cells. Newly made class II molecules carry the invariant chain, which blocks the peptide groove in the endoplasmic reticulum. In the acidified endosome the invariant chain is cut to leave a fragment called CLIP, and HLA-DM exchanges CLIP for antigenic peptide. CD4 binds the beta-2 domain of class II. A mnemonic is the rule of eight: CD8 times MHC class I equals 8, and CD4 times MHC class II equals 8.

Cross-presentation lets some dendritic cells load exogenous antigen on class I, which is how CD8 T cells are primed against viruses that do not infect dendritic cells and against tumors. Superantigens bypass normal processing by binding class II and the T cell receptor beta chain outside the peptide groove, activating many T cells and causing cytokine storms, as in toxic shock syndrome.

HLA type affects disease and transplant matching. Well-known associations include HLA-B27 with ankylosing spondylitis and reactive arthritis, HLA-DR3 and DR4 with type 1 diabetes, HLA-DR4 with rheumatoid arthritis, HLA-DQ2 and DQ8 with celiac disease, and HLA-B*57:01 with abacavir hypersensitivity. Associations are risk modifiers, not diagnoses.

Worked example. A virus blocks TAP. Class I molecules cannot get peptide, surface class I falls, CD8 recognition fails, and NK cells may become active through missing self. Class II presentation remains intact because it does not use TAP.

lessons.title: T Cell Development and the T Cell Receptor
body: T cell precursors leave the bone marrow and enter the thymus, where they develop as thymocytes. Early thymocytes lack CD4 and CD8 (double negative) and then express both (double positive) before becoming single positive CD4 or CD8 cells. Thymic cortex supports early rearrangement and positive selection, and the medulla supports negative selection.

The T cell receptor (TCR) is a heterodimer, most often alpha and beta chains, each with variable and constant regions, associated with the CD3 complex that transmits signals. A minority of T cells use gamma and delta chains. Diversity comes from V(D)J recombination, in which gene segments are joined by the RAG1 and RAG2 recombinases, plus junctional diversity from random nucleotide addition by terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase and imprecise joining. The beta chain rearranges first and is tested through the pre-TCR. Allelic exclusion ensures that one cell expresses one receptor specificity. Defects in RAG cause severe combined immunodeficiency, and the less severe hypomorphic variants cause Omenn syndrome.

Positive selection occurs in the cortex. Double positive thymocytes whose TCRs bind self MHC with at least modest affinity receive survival signals, and those that cannot bind self MHC die by neglect. This selection produces MHC-restricted cells and decides lineage: recognition of class I produces CD8 cells, and recognition of class II produces CD4 cells. Negative selection occurs largely at the corticomedullary junction and in the medulla. Thymocytes that bind self peptide-MHC with high affinity undergo apoptosis. Medullary thymic epithelial cells express many tissue-specific antigens, such as insulin, under control of the transcription factor AIRE. Loss of AIRE causes autoimmune polyendocrinopathy with candidiasis and ectodermal dystrophy because self-reactive cells escape. Some self-reactive CD4 cells instead become regulatory T cells expressing FOXP3.

Only a small minority of thymocytes survive. Thymic development depends on the thymic epithelium, which arises from the third pharyngeal pouch, together with the parathyroids, so 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge syndrome) can cause thymic hypoplasia, hypocalcemia from absent parathyroids, and cardiac outflow defects. Mature naive T cells, with markers such as CD45RA and CCR7, recirculate through lymph nodes and spleen, searching for the rare antigen that matches their receptor, and they depend on homeostatic signals such as IL-7 and weak contact with self MHC to survive until they meet it.

Worked example. A newborn has a conotruncal cardiac defect, seizures from hypocalcemia, and low T cell counts on a newborn screen. This points to 22q11.2 deletion, with reduced thymic output and normal B cell numbers.

lessons.title: T Cell Activation and Effector Subsets
body: Full activation of a naive T cell needs three signals. Signal 1 is TCR engagement of peptide-MHC, with CD4 or CD8 as coreceptor. Signal 2 is costimulation, chiefly CD28 on the T cell binding B7 (CD80 and CD86) on the antigen-presenting cell. Signal 3 is cytokines that direct differentiation. Signal 1 without signal 2 leaves the cell anergic, which is one way of maintaining peripheral tolerance. Proximal TCR signaling uses Lck, ZAP-70, calcium and calcineurin, and the transcription factor NFAT drives interleukin 2 gene expression. IL-2 supports proliferation of activated T cells through the high-affinity receptor containing CD25.

Inhibitory receptors tune the response. CTLA-4 is induced after activation and competes with CD28 for B7 with higher affinity, so it dampens early priming. PD-1 is upregulated on activated and exhausted T cells and, when it engages PD-L1 or PD-L2 in tissues and tumors, restrains effector function. These are the targets of checkpoint inhibitor drugs.

CD4 T helper subsets are defined by cytokine environment and master transcription factors. Th1 cells arise with IL-12 and IFN-gamma, use T-bet, and secrete IFN-gamma to activate macrophages against intracellular pathogens such as mycobacteria. Th2 cells arise with IL-4, use GATA3, and secrete IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13, supporting IgE switching, eosinophils and defense against helminths, and they drive allergic disease. Th17 cells arise with TGF-beta, IL-6 and IL-23, use RORgamma-t, and secrete IL-17 and IL-22 to recruit neutrophils and defend mucosal surfaces against extracellular bacteria and fungi. T follicular helper cells use BCL6 and IL-21 to help B cells in germinal centers. Regulatory T cells use FOXP3, require IL-2, and suppress other cells through IL-10, TGF-beta and CTLA-4. IFN-gamma inhibits Th2 development, and IL-4 inhibits Th1 development.

CD8 cytotoxic T cells recognize class I and kill target cells by delivering perforin and granzymes, which trigger apoptosis through caspases, and by Fas ligand binding Fas on the target. After infection, most effector cells die, and a small pool survives as memory cells. Naive T cells display CD45RA, whereas memory cells express CD45RO. Central memory cells home to lymph nodes, and effector memory cells patrol tissues.

Worked example. A patient has a mutation in IL12RB1 and develops disseminated infection with a nontuberculous mycobacterium after BCG vaccination. Without the IL-12 to IFN-gamma axis, Th1 responses and macrophage activation are weak, so intracellular mycobacteria are not controlled.

lessons.title: B Cells and Antibodies
body: B cells develop in the bone marrow. Heavy chain genes rearrange first, the pre-B receptor tests the heavy chain with surrogate light chains, and light chain genes then rearrange. The result is surface IgM, and later IgD, on immature and mature naive B cells. Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) is needed for pre-B receptor signaling, so X-linked agammaglobulinemia stops development at the pre-B stage and leaves very few circulating B cells.

An immunoglobulin is made of two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains linked by disulfide bonds. Each chain has variable and constant regions. The antigen-binding fragment (Fab) contains the variable regions, and the crystallizable fragment (Fc) mediates effector functions through Fc receptors and complement. Hypervariable segments in the variable region, called complementarity-determining regions, form the antigen contact surface.

The isotypes have distinct roles. IgM is a pentamer, the first antibody made, and the best complement activator. IgG is the most abundant in serum, crosses the placenta through the neonatal Fc receptor, opsonizes microbes and activates complement. IgA is dimeric in secretions, carried across epithelium by the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor, and protects mucosal surfaces and milk. IgE binds mast cells and eosinophils and mediates immediate hypersensitivity and antiparasitic defense. IgD is mainly a B cell surface receptor.

After activation in a lymph node follicle, B cells form germinal centers. There, activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) drives two processes. Somatic hypermutation introduces point mutations in the variable genes, and cells with higher affinity are selected by follicular dendritic cells and T follicular helper cells, giving affinity maturation. Class switch recombination replaces the constant region of the heavy chain while preserving the variable region, so antigen specificity stays the same but the isotype changes. Switching requires CD40 on the B cell binding CD40 ligand on T helper cells, plus cytokines: IL-4 for IgE and IgG4, IFN-gamma for IgG subclasses, and TGF-beta for IgA. Defects in CD40 ligand or AID cause hyper-IgM syndrome. Plasma cells secrete antibody at high rates, and memory B cells persist. T-independent antigens, such as polysaccharide capsules, trigger mostly IgM with limited memory, which is why conjugate vaccines were developed.

Worked example. A boy has recurrent sinopulmonary infections, normal IgM, and very low IgG, IgA and IgE. Lymph nodes lack germinal centers, and his T cells fail to express CD40 ligand. His B cells cannot class switch, which fits hyper-IgM syndrome from CD40L deficiency.

lessons.title: Cytokines and Their Receptors
body: Cytokines are small secreted proteins that act on nearby or distant cells through specific receptors. They can act on the cell that made them (autocrine), on neighbors (paracrine), or throughout the body (endocrine). Individual cytokines are pleiotropic, meaning one cytokine has several effects, and redundant, meaning several cytokines can produce the same effect. Chemokines are a related family that direct cell migration.

You should know a core set. IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-alpha, made mainly by macrophages, drive fever and acute-phase responses, and TNF-alpha also maintains granulomas and causes septic shock when released in excess. IL-2, made by activated T cells, drives T cell proliferation and supports regulatory T cells. IL-4 drives Th2 differentiation and IgE switching. IL-5 recruits and activates eosinophils and supports IgA production. IL-10 and TGF-beta are anti-inflammatory. IL-12 from macrophages and dendritic cells drives Th1 cells and NK activity. IFN-gamma activates macrophages and promotes class I and II expression. IL-17 recruits neutrophils. IL-3 and GM-CSF support hematopoiesis, and IL-7 supports lymphocyte development. Type I interferons induce an antiviral state.

Many cytokine receptors lack intrinsic enzyme activity and signal through Janus kinases (JAKs) that phosphorylate STAT transcription factors, which dimerize and move into the nucleus. The common gamma chain is shared by receptors for IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15 and IL-21, and it signals through JAK3. Mutations in the common gamma chain cause X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency, and JAK3 mutations cause an autosomal recessive form with the same T-negative, NK-negative, B-positive pattern. IL-12 and IFN-gamma signal through STAT4 and STAT1 respectively. Small molecule JAK inhibitors, such as tofacitinib, are used in rheumatoid arthritis and other diseases. Because they dampen many cytokine signals, they raise the risk of infections such as herpes zoster and require attention to cardiovascular and thrombotic risk as stated in drug labeling.

Biologics block specific cytokines. TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept) treat rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease and psoriasis, but impair granuloma maintenance and so can reactivate latent tuberculosis, so patients are screened before treatment. Anakinra blocks the IL-1 receptor. Tocilizumab blocks the IL-6 receptor. Ustekinumab blocks the shared p40 subunit of IL-12 and IL-23. Secukinumab blocks IL-17A. Dupilumab blocks the IL-4 receptor alpha chain, which blocks IL-4 and IL-13 signaling, and mepolizumab targets IL-5. Recombinant IL-2 and interferons are used therapeutically in selected diseases.

Worked example. A patient with rheumatoid arthritis on a TNF inhibitor develops fever, night sweats and an upper lobe cavitary lesion. Loss of TNF-dependent granuloma integrity reactivated latent tuberculosis, which explains why screening precedes treatment.

lessons.title: Immunologic Tolerance
body: Immunologic tolerance is the ability to avoid reacting to self antigens and harmless foreign antigens such as food and commensals. Because receptor generation is random, many lymphocytes are self-reactive, so tolerance has to be actively built and maintained at several checkpoints.

Central tolerance occurs in the primary lymphoid organs. In the thymus, T cells that bind self peptide-MHC strongly are eliminated by negative selection, helped by AIRE-driven display of tissue antigens in the medulla. Some become natural regulatory T cells. In the bone marrow, immature B cells that bind self antigen strongly are handled by receptor editing, in which light chain rearrangement is repeated to change specificity, and, if that fails, by clonal deletion or anergy. Central tolerance is incomplete, since the thymus and marrow cannot display every self antigen.

Peripheral tolerance backs up central tolerance. Anergy occurs when a T cell encounters antigen without costimulation, so it becomes unresponsive, and costimulation is normally absent on resting tissue cells and immature dendritic cells. Activation-induced cell death occurs through Fas and Fas ligand, and defects in Fas cause autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome, with lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly and autoimmune cytopenias. Inhibitory receptors, CTLA-4 and PD-1, limit activation. Regulatory T cells, which express CD4, CD25 and the transcription factor FOXP3, suppress effector cells through IL-10, TGF-beta, CTLA-4 and consumption of IL-2. Mutations in FOXP3 cause IPEX syndrome (immune dysregulation, polyendocrinopathy, enteropathy, X-linked), a disease of infancy with severe diarrhea, early-onset diabetes and eczema. Immune privileged sites, such as the eye, testis and brain, limit immune access, and if sequestered antigens are released after trauma, as in sympathetic ophthalmia, tolerance can fail.

Oral tolerance is the tendency of the gut-associated immune system to respond to dietary antigens with regulatory T cells and IgA instead of inflammation. B cell tolerance has similar mechanisms, but B cells that are anergic have a shortened life span. Tolerance also needs periodic reinforcement, and a breakdown can be triggered by infection, tissue damage, molecular mimicry, or genetic risk.

Molecular mimicry means that a microbial antigen resembles a self antigen, so a response to the microbe cross-reacts with the host. Rheumatic fever after group A streptococcal pharyngitis, with antibodies to M protein cross-reacting with cardiac myosin, is the classic example. Epitope spreading is the broadening of an immune response from an initial target to others on the same tissue.

Worked example. A male infant has watery diarrhea, eczema and type 1 diabetes in the first months of life. He has an FOXP3 mutation. Without regulatory T cells, peripheral tolerance fails and autoreactive effector cells attack multiple organs.

lessons.title: Hypersensitivity Types I and II
body: Hypersensitivity reactions are immune responses that cause tissue injury. The Gell and Coombs scheme sorts them into four types by mechanism. Types I, II and III are antibody mediated, and type IV is T cell mediated.

Type I (immediate) hypersensitivity depends on IgE. In sensitization, a first exposure to allergen drives a Th2 response with IL-4 and IL-13, and B cells switch to IgE. IgE binds the high-affinity receptor FcεRI on mast cells and basophils. On re-exposure, allergen cross-links IgE on the cell, which triggers degranulation within minutes. Preformed mediators, such as histamine and tryptase, cause vasodilation, increased permeability, bronchoconstriction and gut smooth muscle contraction. Newly made mediators, including leukotrienes C4, D4 and E4 and prostaglandin D2, sustain the response, and a late-phase reaction hours later is driven by eosinophils and Th2 cells. Clinical forms include allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis, allergic asthma, urticaria, food allergy and anaphylaxis. Anaphylaxis is a systemic reaction with hypotension, airway involvement and urticaria, and epinephrine is first-line treatment. Elevated serum tryptase supports mast cell activation. Diagnosis uses skin prick testing and specific IgE assays. Allergen immunotherapy shifts the response toward IgG4 and regulatory T cells. Omalizumab binds free IgE, and a nonallergic mechanism of mast cell activation, such as with opioids or radiocontrast, produces anaphylactoid reactions without IgE.

Type II hypersensitivity involves IgG or IgM binding antigens on the surface of cells or the extracellular matrix. Injury arises through complement activation and the membrane attack complex, opsonization and phagocytosis (such as splenic removal of antibody-coated cells), and antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity. Examples include autoimmune hemolytic anemia, immune thrombocytopenia, hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn from maternal antibodies against Rh D, and transfusion reactions with ABO incompatibility. Goodpasture syndrome has antibodies to the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen in glomerular and alveolar basement membranes, and produces linear immunofluorescence. Not all type II diseases kill cells. In Graves disease, antibodies stimulate the TSH receptor, and in myasthenia gravis, antibodies block or deplete the acetylcholine receptor. Pemphigus vulgaris, with antibodies to desmoglein 3, shows intercellular deposition of IgG on immunofluorescence.
A direct Coombs test detects antibody or complement on the patient's own red cells, and an indirect Coombs test detects free antibody in serum that binds reagent red cells.

Worked example. A 22-year-old develops fever, back pain and dark urine minutes into a transfusion. Preformed anti-A or anti-B IgM bound donor cells and activated complement, causing intravascular hemolysis, a type II reaction. The transfusion is stopped immediately.

lessons.title: Hypersensitivity Types III and IV
body: Type III hypersensitivity is caused by antigen-antibody complexes that are not cleared and deposit in tissues. The complexes activate complement through the classical pathway and recruit neutrophils, which release enzymes and oxygen radicals that injure vessel walls, a process producing vasculitis, glomerulonephritis and arthritis. Deposition is favored where blood is filtered under pressure, such as glomeruli and synovium. Injury needs slight antigen excess, because complexes that are very large are removed by the mononuclear phagocyte system and very small ones are not pathogenic. Histology shows fibrinoid necrosis, and immunofluorescence shows granular deposits of immunoglobulin and complement. Complement is consumed, so C3 and C4 are low during active disease.

Systemic forms include serum sickness, which appears 1 to 2 weeks after exposure to a foreign protein or drug such as antithymocyte globulin or some antibiotics, with fever, rash, arthralgia and low complement. Systemic lupus erythematosus, poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis and polyarteritis nodosa associated with hepatitis B are further examples. The Arthus reaction is a local type III reaction at a site of antigen injection in a previously sensitized person, appearing over hours with edema and necrosis, and it can occur after repeated tetanus booster vaccines given too frequently.

Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity is mediated by T cells, not antibody, and appears 48 to 72 hours after exposure. It has no role for complement in its core mechanism and it cannot be transferred by serum but only by cells. There are several forms. In delayed-type hypersensitivity, Th1 cells release IFN-gamma that activates macrophages, and chronic activation produces granulomas, as in tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, Crohn disease and tuberculin skin reactions. In contact dermatitis, haptens such as nickel, poison ivy urushiol or latex bind self proteins and are presented to sensitized T cells, causing eczematous inflammation at the site of contact. In direct cytotoxic reactions, CD8 cells kill target cells, and this mechanism contributes to graft rejection, some drug eruptions, and type 1 diabetes. Severe cutaneous reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, have a T cell mediated component, and HLA associations exist, such as HLA-B*15:02 with carbamazepine in people of Han Chinese ancestry.

The tuberculin skin test and interferon-gamma release assays use this immune memory. A positive tuberculin test shows prior sensitization and does not distinguish latent infection from active disease and may be positive after BCG, while a release assay is not affected by BCG vaccination.

Worked example. A 30-year-old develops an itchy, vesicular rash on the wrist and under the watch clasp 2 days after wearing a new watch. Nickel acts as a hapten, sensitized T cells respond on re-exposure, and the delayed timing with eczematous skin changes identifies a type IV reaction.

lessons.title: Autoimmune Disease: Mechanisms and Markers
body: Autoimmune disease results when the adaptive immune system attacks self tissue. It requires a combination of genetic susceptibility, an environmental trigger and failed tolerance. Women are affected far more often than men in most systemic autoimmune diseases. HLA alleles are the strongest single genetic contributors, although other genes, such as PTPN22, CTLA4 and complement genes, also matter. Triggers include infections (molecular mimicry, epitope spreading, bystander activation), tissue injury that exposes sequestered antigens, drugs, and hormones. Mechanistically, tissue damage may be caused by autoantibodies (types II and III) or by autoreactive T cells (type IV). Organ-specific diseases target one tissue, and systemic diseases involve many.

The autoantibody profile is central to diagnosis. Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) are sensitive for systemic lupus erythematosus but are not specific, since they occur in other connective tissue disease and in healthy people, especially at low titer. Anti-double-stranded DNA and anti-Smith antibodies are specific for lupus, and anti-dsDNA titers track with nephritis. Anti-histone antibodies suggest drug-induced lupus, with drugs such as hydralazine and procainamide. Antiphospholipid antibodies cause thrombosis and pregnancy loss, and they can prolong aPTT in vitro. Rheumatoid arthritis shows rheumatoid factor (IgM against the Fc of IgG) and, more specifically, anti-citrullinated protein antibodies. Anti-centromere antibodies are associated with limited scleroderma (CREST), and anti-topoisomerase I (Scl-70) with diffuse scleroderma. Anti-SSA (Ro) and anti-SSB (La) occur in Sjogren syndrome, and anti-SSA is linked to neonatal lupus with congenital heart block. Anti-Jo-1 is associated with antisynthetase syndrome and myositis. ANCA types separate vasculitides: c-ANCA (proteinase 3) in granulomatosis with polyangiitis and p-ANCA (myeloperoxidase) in microscopic polyangiitis and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Anti-mitochondrial antibodies identify primary biliary cholangitis. Anti-tissue transglutaminase and anti-endomysial IgA identify celiac disease, and IgA deficiency can cause false negatives. Anti-smooth muscle antibodies are seen in autoimmune hepatitis.

Organ-specific examples illustrate mechanisms. In Graves disease, stimulating antibodies to the TSH receptor cause hyperthyroidism. In Hashimoto thyroiditis, T cell infiltration and anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies cause hypothyroidism. In myasthenia gravis, antibodies to the acetylcholine receptor cause fatigable weakness, and thymoma or thymic hyperplasia may be present. In type 1 diabetes, T cell destruction of beta cells occurs with autoantibodies to insulin, GAD65 and islet antigens. Multiple sclerosis involves T cell mediated attack on CNS myelin. Pernicious anemia involves antibodies to intrinsic factor and parietal cells.
Treatment strategies aim to remove the cause, replace the lost function, and suppress the response with corticosteroids, antimetabolites, B cell depletion with rituximab, or cytokine blockade.

Worked example. A 30-year-old woman has a malar rash, arthralgias, proteinuria and low C3 and C4. Anti-dsDNA is high. Her antibodies form complexes that deposit in the kidney, so a renal biopsy is needed to define the class of lupus nephritis and guide therapy.

lessons.title: Primary Antibody and B Cell Deficiencies
body: Primary immunodeficiencies are inherited disorders of immune function, and a first step in diagnosis is to match the infection pattern to the arm of the immune system that is failing. Antibody deficiencies, the most common group, typically present after maternal IgG wanes at about 6 months of age, with recurrent sinopulmonary infections caused by encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae, plus enteroviruses and Giardia. Fungal and intracellular infections are less prominent because T cells are intact.

X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton) arises from BTK mutations that block pre-B cell maturation, so there are few or no CD19 positive B cells, and all immunoglobulin classes are low. Lymph nodes and tonsils are small because follicles lack B cells. Affected boys are well until about 6 months, then develop recurrent bacterial infections. Treatment is lifelong immunoglobulin replacement, and live vaccines such as oral polio are avoided. Intact T cell function means that most viral infections are handled, but enteroviral disease can be severe.

Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) is a heterogeneous group of disorders with low IgG and low IgA or IgM, normal or low B cell numbers and impaired vaccine responses. Presentation is usually in the second or third decade, with sinopulmonary infections, autoimmunity such as cytopenias, granulomatous disease and lymphoid hyperplasia, an increased risk of lymphoma and gastric cancer, and chronic giardiasis. It is a diagnosis of exclusion after other causes of hypogammaglobulinemia are removed. Management includes immunoglobulin replacement.

Selective IgA deficiency is the most common primary immunodeficiency. Many patients are asymptomatic, whereas others have sinopulmonary and gastrointestinal infections, giardiasis, celiac disease and allergy. Patients with anti-IgA antibodies may have anaphylaxis when given blood products containing IgA, so washed cells or IgA-deficient donors may be used.

Hyper-IgM syndrome is most often caused by CD40 ligand mutations on T cells, which is X-linked, or CD40 or AID defects, which are autosomal. IgM is normal or high while IgG, IgA and IgE are low. The T cell defect also impairs macrophage activation, so patients have opportunistic infections with Pneumocystis jirovecii and Cryptosporidium in addition to bacterial infections.

Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy reflects delayed onset of the infant's own antibody production and resolves on its own, and it is distinguished from permanent defects by normal vaccine responses over time.

Worked example. A 14-month-old boy has had four episodes of otitis media and two pneumonias. His mother's brother died of infection in childhood. Flow cytometry shows no CD19 positive cells, and total IgG is very low. A BTK mutation is the likely finding, and immunoglobulin replacement lowers his infection rate.

lessons.title: Primary T Cell, Combined and Phagocyte Defects
body: T cell defects present earlier than antibody defects, often in the first months, with failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea, persistent thrush, and opportunistic infections with Pneumocystis jirovecii, cytomegalovirus and other viruses and fungi. Live vaccines can cause disease. Because B cells depend on T cell help, combined defects follow.

Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) is a pediatric emergency, with absent or very poor T cell function and impaired antibody production. The most common form is X-linked, from a common gamma chain mutation, giving T-negative, B-positive, NK-negative cells. Adenosine deaminase deficiency causes accumulation of toxic metabolites in lymphocytes and gives T-negative, B-negative, NK-negative cells with skeletal abnormalities. RAG1 and RAG2 defects give T-negative, B-negative, NK-positive cells. A thymic shadow is usually absent, and the lymphocyte count is very low. Newborn screening uses T cell receptor excision circles, which are lower when thymic output is poor. The treatment is hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, gene therapy in selected types, and enzyme replacement for adenosine deaminase deficiency. Irradiated blood products and avoidance of live vaccines are required.

Other syndromes have recognizable features. DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion) presents with hypocalcemia, cardiac defects and thymic hypoplasia. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is X-linked, with eczema, thrombocytopenia with small platelets, and recurrent infections, and it is caused by WAS gene mutations affecting actin cytoskeleton. Ataxia-telangiectasia is caused by ATM mutations that impair DNA double-strand break repair, producing cerebellar ataxia, telangiectasias, sinopulmonary infections, low IgA and raised alpha-fetoprotein, with a risk of lymphoid malignancy and radiosensitivity. Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis can reflect Th17 or IL-17 pathway defects. Hyper-IgE syndrome (Job syndrome, STAT3 mutation) shows coarse facies, retained primary teeth, cold staphylococcal abscesses, eczema and fractures, with very high IgE. Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease reflects defects in the IL-12 to IFN-gamma axis. Bare lymphocyte syndrome type II lacks MHC class II expression and leads to a CD4 deficiency.

Phagocyte defects present with skin and organ abscesses, delayed wound healing and fungal infection. Chronic granulomatous disease (NADPH oxidase), leukocyte adhesion deficiency (CD18) and Chediak-Higashi syndrome (LYST mutation, defective lysosomal trafficking with giant granules, partial albinism, neuropathy and infections) are the key examples. Complement and asplenia are other branches of the work-up.

Worked example. A 5-year-old boy has eczema, recurrent ear infections and easy bruising. His platelet count is low, with small platelets on smear. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is the diagnosis, and bleeding, infection and autoimmunity are managed until stem cell transplant is considered.

lessons.title: Secondary Immunodeficiency and HIV
body: Secondary (acquired) immunodeficiency is far more common than primary disease. Causes include malnutrition, the most common worldwide, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, liver cirrhosis, hematologic malignancy, splenectomy or functional asplenia in sickle cell disease, protein-losing states such as nephrotic syndrome and enteropathy, and drugs. Glucocorticoids, cytotoxic drugs, anti-CD20 antibodies, TNF inhibitors and calcineurin inhibitors each leave a characteristic pattern of risk. Asplenia predisposes to infection with encapsulated organisms, so vaccination against pneumococcus, meningococcus and Haemophilus influenzae type b is recommended.

HIV is a retrovirus that infects cells carrying CD4 and a coreceptor, either CCR5 or CXCR4. Early infection typically uses CCR5, which explains why people homozygous for a CCR5 deletion are relatively resistant. The envelope glycoproteins gp120 and gp41 mediate binding and fusion. Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from the viral RNA, integrase inserts it into the host genome, and protease cleaves viral polyproteins into functional proteins. The virus establishes latent reservoirs in resting memory CD4 T cells. Progressive loss of CD4 T cells, from direct viral killing and chronic immune activation, impairs cell-mediated immunity.

Acute infection may produce a mononucleosis-like illness with fever, rash and lymphadenopathy 2 to 4 weeks after exposure. After a clinically quiet phase, falling CD4 counts bring opportunistic disease. Risk categories are approximate, but Pneumocystis pneumonia appears below about 200 cells per microliter, and Mycobacterium avium complex and disseminated cytomegalovirus below about 50. AIDS is defined by a CD4 count below 200 cells per microliter or by an AIDS-defining illness.

Diagnosis uses a fourth-generation antigen and antibody combination assay, which detects p24 antigen as well as antibodies, followed by a differentiation assay and nucleic acid testing when needed. In the window period, RNA testing detects infection earlier than antibody tests. In infants born to infected mothers, antibody tests are unreliable because of maternal IgG, so nucleic acid tests are used. Antiretroviral therapy, combining agents from classes such as integrase strand transfer inhibitors, nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, protease inhibitors, entry inhibitors and CCR5 antagonists, suppresses viral load, restores CD4 counts, and prevents transmission when sustained viral suppression is achieved. Current guidelines recommend treatment for all people with HIV, regardless of CD4 count, and HLA-B*57:01 testing before abacavir. Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome can occur after starting therapy, when recovering immunity reacts to an existing infection.

Worked example. A 35-year-old man has weeks of dry cough, exertional dyspnea and oral thrush. His CD4 count is 90 cells per microliter, and chest imaging shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Pneumocystis pneumonia is likely, and prophylaxis and antiretroviral therapy are indicated as part of treatment.

lessons.title: Transplantation Immunology
body: Transplant rejection is an adaptive immune response to allogeneic antigens, mainly polymorphic HLA molecules. Recipient T cells recognize donor HLA in two ways. In direct allorecognition, recipient T cells bind intact donor HLA on donor antigen-presenting cells, and a large fraction of T cells cross-react, which explains the intensity of the early response. In indirect allorecognition, recipient antigen-presenting cells process donor HLA peptides and present them on recipient MHC, and this route dominates chronic rejection.

Rejection is classified by timing and mechanism. Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes to hours because the recipient has preformed antibodies, from earlier transfusion, pregnancy or transplant, or from ABO incompatibility. Complement activation and thrombosis in graft vessels cause rapid ischemic necrosis. Crossmatching and ABO matching are designed to prevent it. Acute rejection occurs days to months after transplant. Acute cellular rejection is T cell mediated, with lymphocytic infiltrate and tubulitis in a kidney graft, and it responds to increased immunosuppression. Acute antibody-mediated rejection is a type II reaction with donor-specific antibodies, complement deposition (C4d staining) and vascular injury. Chronic rejection develops over months to years and shows graft arteriosclerosis, interstitial fibrosis, and, in kidney grafts, glomerulopathy, bronchiolitis obliterans in lungs, and vasculopathy in hearts. It responds poorly to treatment.

Matching has several layers. ABO compatibility is required for solid organs in most cases. HLA matching counts most for HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-DR in kidney transplantation. The crossmatch tests recipient serum against donor cells to detect donor-specific antibodies, and panel reactive antibody testing estimates how broadly sensitized a recipient is. Some sites, including the cornea and brain, are immune privileged, so grafts often succeed without matching.

Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) occurs when donor immune cells, mostly in bone marrow or stem cell transplants, attack recipient tissue. It needs an immunocompetent graft, a recipient unable to reject it, and HLA disparity. Acute GVHD typically damages skin (maculopapular rash), liver (cholestasis) and gut (diarrhea), and chronic GVHD resembles scleroderma-like or lupus-like autoimmune disease. A modest graft-versus-leukemia effect is therapeutically useful.

Immunosuppressants target pathways in T cell activation. Cyclosporine and tacrolimus inhibit calcineurin and so reduce IL-2 transcription, and they cause nephrotoxicity, hypertension and, for tacrolimus, new-onset diabetes. Sirolimus and everolimus inhibit mTOR and block IL-2 signaling. Mycophenolate inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase, which impairs purine synthesis in proliferating lymphocytes. Azathioprine is a purine analog, and its toxicity is increased by allopurinol and affected by TPMT activity. Corticosteroids reduce cytokine gene expression. Basiliximab blocks CD25, and antithymocyte globulin depletes T cells. Belatacept blocks CD28 costimulation. All raise infection and cancer risk.

Worked example. A kidney recipient has a rising creatinine 5 months after transplant. Biopsy shows lymphocytic tubulitis without C4d, so acute cellular rejection is likely, and treatment is pulse corticosteroids with consideration of T cell depleting therapy if severe.

lessons.title: Tumor Immunology and Immunotherapy
body: The immune system can recognize and eliminate some tumors, a process called immunosurveillance. The more complete concept is cancer immunoediting, with three phases: elimination, in which immune cells destroy transformed cells, equilibrium, in which the tumor is held in check while variants arise, and escape, in which resistant clones grow. Evidence that immunity matters includes the higher cancer risk in people with immunodeficiency or long-term immunosuppression, especially virus-associated cancers and skin cancers, the presence of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, and the efficacy of immunotherapy.

Tumor antigens include tumor-specific neoantigens from mutations, tumor-associated antigens that are overexpressed normal proteins such as HER2, oncofetal antigens (alpha-fetoprotein and carcinoembryonic antigen), cancer-testis antigens, and viral antigens from oncogenic viruses such as HPV and EBV. Neoantigen burden helps explain why tumors with many mutations, such as melanoma and mismatch-repair-deficient cancers, often respond to immunotherapy. Oncofetal antigens are useful as markers for monitoring but not for screening or diagnosis alone.

Tumors escape in several ways. They downregulate MHC class I or antigen processing machinery, which hides them from CD8 T cells, although this may expose them to NK cells. They express PD-L1, secrete TGF-beta and IL-10, recruit regulatory T cells and myeloid-derived suppressor cells, and lose antigens under selective pressure.

Immune checkpoint inhibitors release natural brakes on T cells. Ipilimumab blocks CTLA-4. Pembrolizumab and nivolumab block PD-1, and atezolizumab, durvalumab and avelumab block PD-L1. They are used in melanoma, non-small cell lung cancer, renal cell carcinoma, Hodgkin lymphoma and tumors with mismatch repair deficiency, among others. Their characteristic toxicities are immune-related adverse events, including colitis, pneumonitis, hepatitis, dermatitis, and endocrinopathies such as thyroiditis, hypophysitis and adrenal insufficiency. These are managed by holding the drug and giving corticosteroids, and hormone replacement is needed for endocrine failure.

Other immunotherapies include monoclonal antibodies that mediate antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity, such as rituximab against CD20 and trastuzumab against HER2, and bispecific antibodies that link T cells to tumor cells. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells are the patient's own T cells engineered to express a receptor combining an antibody-derived binding domain with signaling domains. CD19-directed CAR T cells are used in some B cell leukemias and lymphomas. Toxicities include cytokine release syndrome, with fever and hypotension that may be treated with tocilizumab, neurotoxicity, and prolonged B cell aplasia that requires immunoglobulin replacement. Intravesical BCG for bladder cancer is an older immunotherapy.

Worked example. A patient on pembrolizumab for lung cancer develops profuse diarrhea and abdominal pain 8 weeks after starting treatment. Immune-related colitis is likely, and infection is excluded while corticosteroids are started.

lessons.title: Vaccines and Passive Immunity
body: A vaccine trains adaptive immunity to recognize a pathogen without causing disease, so that memory cells respond rapidly on real exposure. The first (primary) response to an antigen appears after about one to two weeks and is mostly IgM with a modest IgG component. The secondary (anamnestic) response is faster, larger, higher in affinity, and dominated by IgG and, at mucosal sites, IgA, because memory B cells have already undergone switching and affinity maturation.

Vaccine types differ in their immunology. Live attenuated vaccines, such as measles, mumps, rubella, varicella, yellow fever, rotavirus and the intranasal influenza vaccine, replicate and stimulate strong humoral and cellular responses, often with a single or few doses. They are generally contraindicated in pregnancy and severe immunodeficiency because the vaccine organism could cause disease. Inactivated vaccines (injected polio, hepatitis A, rabies) and subunit, toxoid and recombinant vaccines (hepatitis B surface antigen, tetanus and diphtheria toxoids, human papillomavirus virus-like particles) cannot replicate, so they are safe in immunocompromised people but may need boosters and adjuvants. Polysaccharide vaccines elicit T-independent responses with poor memory and weak responses in young children. Conjugate vaccines link the polysaccharide to a carrier protein, so T helper cells enable class switching and memory, which is the principle behind Haemophilus influenzae type b, pneumococcal conjugate and meningococcal conjugate vaccines. Messenger RNA vaccines deliver nucleic acid encoding an antigen, and adjuvants such as aluminum salts activate innate pathways and promote uptake by antigen-presenting cells.

Herd immunity occurs when enough of a population is immune that transmission chains break, protecting those who cannot be vaccinated. The threshold depends on how contagious the disease is, so it is higher for measles than for diseases with lower transmissibility. Vaccination policy is contested at the margins of mandates and schedules, but scientific consensus supports the safety and effectiveness of the routine schedules recommended by national advisory bodies, and, as of this writing, the details of schedules should be checked against current official recommendations.

Passive immunity is the transfer of ready-made antibody. Natural passive immunity comes from maternal IgG across the placenta and IgA in breast milk, and it wanes over months. Artificial passive immunity uses immunoglobulin products such as hepatitis B immune globulin, rabies immune globulin, tetanus immune globulin, and monoclonal antibodies. It gives immediate but temporary protection and no memory. Post-exposure prophylaxis for rabies combines passive antibody and active vaccine because the vaccine takes time to work.

Worked example. An unvaccinated child has a deep contaminated wound. Tetanus immune globulin provides immediate antitoxin, while tetanus toxoid vaccine starts active immunity at a different injection site, because the toxoid alone would take days to produce protective antibody.

lessons.title: Laboratory Methods in Clinical Immunology
body: Immunologic laboratory tests rely on the specificity of antibody-antigen binding, and a good clinician understands what each assay measures and how it can mislead.

The enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) detects an antigen or antibody in a sample. In a direct or sandwich format, a capture antibody on a plate binds antigen, and a labeled detection antibody gives a color change proportional to the amount present. In an indirect format, antigen on the plate captures patient antibody, which is detected with an enzyme-linked anti-human antibody. ELISA is used for HIV screening, hormone levels and cytokine measurement. False positives can arise from cross-reactivity, and false negatives from the window period or the hook effect, in which extreme antigen excess saturates both antibodies and lowers the signal.

Flow cytometry labels cells with fluorescent antibodies and measures them one at a time as they pass a laser, so it counts and phenotypes cells by surface markers. It is used for CD4 counts in HIV, to identify leukemia and lymphoma by marker pattern, to detect CD55 and CD59 loss in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, and to run the dihydrorhodamine test for chronic granulomatous disease. Immunofluorescence on tissue sections shows patterns: linear staining along basement membranes in anti-GBM disease, and granular staining in immune complex disease. Immunohistochemistry uses enzyme-labeled antibodies on tissue.

Blotting methods separate molecules by size. Southern blotting detects DNA, northern blotting detects RNA, and western blotting detects proteins with antibodies. Western blotting has been used to confirm HIV antibody results, though current algorithms use differentiation immunoassays and nucleic acid tests. Polymerase chain reaction amplifies nucleic acid sequences and is used to detect pathogens and to type HLA alleles.

Serum protein electrophoresis separates proteins by charge and shows a sharp spike in the gamma region when a single plasma cell clone produces a monoclonal protein. Immunofixation identifies the heavy and light chain type, and serum free light chain assays add sensitivity. A polyclonal increase appears as a broad gamma band in chronic inflammation and cirrhosis. Complement tests include C3 and C4 levels and the CH50 total hemolytic complement assay, which screens the classical pathway and terminal components. Low C3 and C4 suggest classical pathway consumption, as in lupus nephritis, and low C3 with normal C4 suggests alternative pathway activation, as in some forms of glomerulonephritis. Absent CH50 with normal C3 and C4 suggests a terminal component defect.

Transfusion and transplant testing includes ABO and Rh typing, antibody screens (indirect Coombs), and crossmatching. Direct Coombs detects antibody on a patient's own red cells. HLA typing uses PCR-based sequencing methods, and the flow or bead-based crossmatch detects donor-specific antibody. Skin prick and intradermal testing detect IgE sensitization, and patch testing evaluates contact (type IV) allergy. Tryptase measurement after a suspected reaction supports mast cell activation.

Worked example. A 60-year-old has anemia, back pain and renal failure. Serum protein electrophoresis shows a gamma spike, and immunofixation identifies an IgG kappa band, which fits a plasma cell neoplasm and prompts bone marrow evaluation.
